entries.title: Native Plants of North Georgia: A Photo Guide for Plant Enthusiasts (UGA Extension B 1339)
entries.framing: Written for the elevation, slope, and zone conditions of Pickens County — closer to this slope than any statewide guide.

entries.title: Native Plants for Georgia, Part I: Trees, Shrubs, and Woody Vines (UGA Extension B 987)
entries.framing: Directly covers most woody species already tracked — White Pine, native azaleas, dogwood, mountain laurel, oakleaf hydrangea, holly — with native-status notes and culture requirements.

entries.title: Native Plants for Georgia, Part III: Wildflowers (UGA Extension B 987-3)
entries.framing: Spec sheet for siting native ornamentals as the dashboard expands. The "shaded woodland adjacent to streams" framing matches the wooded ridge/cove conditions on Church Mountain Road.

entries.title: Native Plants for Georgia, Part II: Ferns (UGA Extension B 987-2)
entries.framing: Shaded north-facing slopes at 2,873 ft routinely host Christmas fern, New York fern, and rattlesnake fern — natural additions to a habitat-focused dashboard.

entries.title: UGA Extension — Pickens County Office
entries.framing: The actual front door for ground-truthing the property — soil samples and pest IDs go through here.

entries.title: Pollinator Garden Design Guide (UGA Extension B 1570-1)
entries.framing: Translates the "support local wildlife" goal into actionable plant combinations vetted for Georgia.

entries.title: Selecting Trees and Shrubs as Resources for Pollinators (UGA Extension B 1483)
entries.framing: Bridges the dashboard's woody-plant focus (azalea, hydrangea, mountain laurel, holly, dogwood) with the pollinator goal.

entries.title: Beyond Butterflies: Gardening for Native Pollinators (UGA Extension B 1349)
entries.framing: "Indigenous wildlife" extends to native bees and other invertebrates that don't show up in glossier guides.

entries.title: Eco-Friendly Garden: Attracting Pollinators, Beneficial Insects, and Other Natural Predators (UGA Extension B 1456)
entries.framing: Speaks to a "field journal, low-intervention" management philosophy — habitat structure over sprays.

entries.title: Connect to Protect — UGA State Botanical Garden of Georgia
entries.framing: Direct sourcing path for Georgia-genotype native plant material.

entries.title: Mimsie Lanier Center for Native Plant Studies (UGA SBG)
entries.framing: The serious end of "indigenous-first" — ecotype-correct seed and rare-plant propagation.

entries.title: Native Trees of Georgia (Georgia Forestry Commission)
entries.framing: Self-contained tree ID reference at PDF scale — great offline companion for walking the woods. Covers the cove hardwood mix typical of 2,500–3,000 ft Blue Ridge.

entries.title: Georgia Forestry Commission — Forest Stewardship Program
entries.framing: Genuinely tailored guidance for a wooded mountain parcel — far more property-specific than any publication. Plans include wildlife and indigenous-species objectives.

entries.title: Warnell School of Forestry & Natural Resources — Outreach Publications
entries.framing: Georgia-specific coverage of forest health, prescribed fire in Appalachian hardwoods, and wildlife habitat structure — written for the cove hardwood mix that grows here.

entries.title: NC State Extension Gardener Handbook
entries.framing: NC State's mountain-region material is often more directly applicable than UGA's Piedmont-leaning guidance, especially for cool-night/elevated sites.

entries.title: Clemson HGIC — Native Plants for Wildlife Resources
entries.framing: Upstate SC shares southern Appalachian flora with Pickens County GA. Filtering by wildlife outcome matches this dashboard's framing.

entries.title: Lawns in Georgia: Selection and Species (UGA Extension B 1533)
entries.framing: The defensible basis for running the turf as turf-type tall fescue at 2,873 ft, where summers are too cool for Bermuda and far too humid for the creeping bentgrass a golf green would use.

entries.title: Plant Tall Fescue Lawns Now in North Georgia (UGA CAES)
entries.framing: Tall fescue is a bunchgrass — it won't knit over bare spots on its own — so the turf stays full only by overseeding every fall; this anchors the September window in the turf calendar.

entries.title: North Georgia Mountains Chapter — Georgia Native Plant Society
entries.framing: Pickens sits just south of the chapter's stated counties — same species, same soils, same elevations as this slope.

entries.title: Georgia Native Plant Society — Plant of the Year
entries.framing: A curated yearly nudge toward an indigenous species worth adding — a low-pressure recommendation engine that fits the field-journal tone.

entries.title: Audubon Plants for Birds (zip 30143)
entries.framing: Directly bridges the Plants card and Wildlife > Birds tab — for 30143, returns plants ranked by bird value.

entries.title: Native Plant Finder (NWF / Tallamy / Shropshire) — zip 30143
entries.framing: Defensible, science-based answer to "which natives matter most for indigenous wildlife at 30143" — for north Georgia, dominated by oaks (~400+ Lepidoptera), willows, cherries, blueberries.

entries.title: Homegrown National Park (Doug Tallamy)
entries.framing: Philosophical anchor for the entire dashboard — "support local wildlife and plants, especially indigenous" is essentially the Homegrown National Park thesis.

entries.title: Keystone Plants by Ecoregion — National Wildlife Federation
entries.framing: The "if you only plant five things" answer for this specific ecoregion.

entries.title: Mt. Cuba Center — Trial Garden Reports
entries.framing: The Wild Hydrangea report (2022) is directly applicable to the Hydrangea entries — currently ambiguous between native (H. arborescens, H. quercifolia) and non-native (H. macrophylla).

entries.title: Mt. Cuba Wild Hydrangea Top Performers (PDF)
entries.framing: Direct, citable content for the existing Hydrangea entry — far more rigorous than nursery marketing.

entries.title: Xerces Society — Pollinator Conservation Resources: Southeast Region
entries.framing: Their Southeast plant list lands at the property's elevation — the invertebrate-conservation source written for Appalachian conditions.

entries.title: Xerces Society — Pollinator Plants of the Southeast Region (PDF)
entries.framing: Compact enough to live as a printed companion at the homestead; tuned to the species pool the property can host.

entries.title: Georgia Botanical Society (BotSoc)
entries.framing: Trips routinely visit Blue Ridge, Cohutta, and Chattahoochee NF — landscapes ecologically continuous with the property. Tipularia's southern Appalachian articles match the field-journal depth this dashboard wants.

entries.title: Georgia Botanical Society — 2026 Field Trips
entries.framing: Concrete dated events within an hour of Jasper.

entries.title: Atlanta Botanical Garden — Southeastern Center for Conservation
entries.framing: Their North Georgia fieldwork is geographically next door; species lists for at-risk natives are a candidate filter when adding plants. For any rare-species restoration thread, ABG is the propagation-and-safeguarding partner.

entries.title: Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center — Native Plant Database
entries.framing: A reliable per-species page when no UGA bulletin covers what's growing here.

entries.title: Birds Georgia (formerly Georgia Audubon) — Plants for Birds & Wildlife Sanctuary Certification
entries.framing: Cleanest path to a meaningful, low-cost certification recognizing native plantings on Church Mountain Road — and a sourcing channel for hard-to-find Georgia natives.

entries.title: Georgia DNR — Create Backyard Habitat
entries.framing: State-level, free, tonally aligned with the field-journal voice — practical guidance like "mow less, ditch chemicals, plant natives" rather than urgent action lists.

entries.title: Georgia Plant Conservation Alliance (GPCA)
entries.framing: Statewide infrastructure for any "rare plant we'd want to support on this property" path — they can connect a landowner to propagation material, restoration partners, and the right safeguarding contact for any state-listed species.

entries.title: Natural Communities of Georgia (UGA Press companion site)
entries.framing: The reference that answers "what natural community is this slope, and what species belong in it?" Foundation for any restorative planting decision here.

entries.title: GA DNR — "Georgia's Natural Communities and Associated Rare Plant and Animal Species" (PDF)
entries.framing: Direct list of "species worth looking for on this property, or supporting if found" matched to the property's actual community types.

entries.title: GNPS Native Plant Habitat Certification (Silver / Gold)
entries.framing: A second certification track alongside Birds Georgia Wildlife Sanctuary. The two are complementary — Audubon emphasizes bird-habitat plants; GNPS emphasizes native-only composition.

entries.title: American Chestnut Foundation (TACF)
entries.framing: American chestnut was once a dominant canopy species at this elevation in the southern Appalachians. The blight (introduced 1904) killed virtually all mature trees from Maine to Georgia by 1950. This is one of the two big landowner-participation restoration species (the other being eastern hemlock). TACF chapters connect landowners to restoration plantings and seed sources.

entries.title: Hemlock Restoration — HRI + Georgia Forestry Commission HWA Program
entries.framing: If hemlocks exist on the property (very likely at 2,873 ft in cool drainages), there's a direct, recurring, landowner-driven treatment protocol that keeps them alive — and no other native conifer fills hemlock's ecological role.

entries.title: Native plant nurseries — North Georgia / Southeast sourcing
entries.framing: Sourcing matters for restorative work — wild-collection drives some natives toward extinction. Ethical-propagation nurseries are the only acceptable path for rare species.

entries.title: Native warm-season grass and meadow seed — Roundstone & Ernst
entries.framing: The native meadow regime in the meadow is a seed project, not a plant-by-plant one. Regionally-adapted ecotype seed (not generic Midwest stock) is the right provenance for a 2,873 ft Blue Ridge slope.

entries.title: Rewild Your Lawn (UGA CAES)
entries.framing: The through-line for running that ground as meadow rather than turf — UGA's own voice supporting the natural approach, which lands more easily than an advocacy site would.

entries.title: Plant a Wildflower Meadow (Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center)
entries.framing: The practical playbook for the meadow regime — site prep, sowing, and the first-year mow-every-4-to-6-weeks rhythm that holds back weeds while the slow natives root in.

entries.title: Establishing Pollinator Meadows from Seed (Xerces Society)
entries.framing: The meadow's point is the grasses-plus-wildflowers mix that feeds pollinators, not grass alone. This is the seed-and-establishment reference for getting that mix to take in the meadow.

entries.title: Beneficial Buffers: Native Plants for Ponds & Lakes in the South
entries.framing: Fernwood has a drafted `pond-area` zone (type `planted`) and three Sarracenia already in it. This is the buffer-planting half of that zone, and it is written for the South rather than a generic temperate audience. ⚠️ Vendor-authored — treat as a **seed**, and check any species against the UGA/USDA sources in Category 1 before it reaches a card.

entries.title: Wetland Plants of Georgia (iNaturalist guide)
entries.framing: Georgia-specific and photo-first, which is what actually helps at the water's edge. Complements the vendor guide above with observation data rather than sales copy. ⚠️ Returns **403** to automated checks — a bot-block, not a dead link; it loads normally in a browser.

entries.title: Georgia DNR — State Wildlife Action Plan 2025 (Blue Ridge Ecoregion)
entries.framing: The property is in the Blue Ridge ecoregion at 2,873 ft — the SWAP Blue Ridge story map flags the exact mountain-specific SGCN species (salamanders, high-elevation breeding warblers, native trout) the dashboard should care about.

entries.title: eBird — Pickens County, GA (Cornell Lab)
entries.framing: Where the Birds tab's monthsPresent and status fields come from. Pickens County bar charts visualize the same data. Free, public.

entries.title: USFWS IPaC — Information for Planning and Consultation
entries.framing: Authoritative federal species list for the exact Fernwood parcel — most defensible source for any "federally listed species on or near this property" claim.

entries.title: Birds Georgia — Wildlife Sanctuary Program
entries.framing: Directly maps to "support indigenous wildlife and plants" — most concrete Georgia-specific certification with a mailable yard sign.

entries.title: Audubon — Survival by Degrees Climate Visualizer
entries.framing: The property's 2,873 ft elevation is exactly the kind of high-elevation refuge where climate-stressed Appalachian breeders may persist longest.

entries.title: iNaturalist — Pickens County, GA
entries.framing: Covers the amphibians and pollinators eBird doesn't. GA DNR's Wildlife Conservation Section uses iNaturalist data to time surveys for tracked species.

entries.title: Southeast Bumble Bee Atlas (Xerces + GA DNR)
entries.framing: North Georgia mountain populations of native bumble bees (incl. potentially the at-risk American bumble bee, Bombus pensylvanicus) are under-surveyed; the property could adopt a nearby grid cell directly tied to the "support indigenous" goal.

entries.title: USFWS Partners for Fish and Wildlife — Georgia Program
entries.framing: Private land in a high-priority Blue Ridge habitat zone — eligible for free expert site visits and potential cost-share for stream/riparian restoration, native plantings, pollinator meadows.

entries.title: USDA Forest Service — Chattahoochee-Oconee NF Fire & Wildlife Management
entries.framing: Property is near/borders the Chattahoochee NF; prescribed-burn smoke days, post-burn songbird responses, and fire-dependent oak/pine ecology directly affect the property's wildlife calendar and outdoor planning.

entries.title: NestWatch (Cornell Lab)
entries.framing: Mix of forest edge and likely hummingbird/bluebird/wren nest opportunities is ideal NestWatch habitat; natural extension of the Birds tab into breeding-season detail.

entries.title: Project FeederWatch (Cornell Lab + Birds Canada)
entries.framing: Property's elevation puts it in Junco/Purple Finch/White-throated Sparrow winter territory — Pickens County is right at the southern edge of some northern-finch irruption zones.

entries.title: Merlin Bird ID (Cornell Lab)
entries.framing: The property is dense forest where most birds are heard before seen — Merlin Sound ID is the fastest way to validate the Birds tab's species list.

entries.title: FrogWatch USA (AZA)
entries.framing: Property's elevation and likely seeps/streams are prime habitat for spring peeper, gray treefrog, American toad, and possibly mountain chorus frog — all detected by call. Directly populates Amphibians tab monthsActive.

entries.title: SREL Herpetology — UGA Savannah River Ecology Lab
entries.framing: Has dedicated species accounts for the Blue Ridge salamanders/frogs likely on the property (Blue Ridge Two-lined Salamander, Spring Peeper, Gray Treefrog) — better than AmphibiaWeb for GA-specific natural history.

entries.title: Bat Conservation International — Build a Bat House
entries.framing: North Georgia caves/hollows host species hit hard by WNS; a BCI-spec bat house at the property gives displaced colonies a clean alternative.

entries.title: Georgia Biodiversity Portal (GA DNR Natural Heritage)
entries.framing: State-level companion to USFWS IPaC — surfaces state-listed species (not just federally listed) that may occur in Pickens County.

entries.title: Bumble Bees of the Eastern United States (Colla, Richardson & Williams — USFS)
entries.framing: Standard ID reference paired with the SE Bumble Bee Atlas — at 2,873 ft the property is in range of mountain-affiliated species like B. vagans and possibly B. fervidus.

entries.title: Hummingbirds at Home (National Audubon)
entries.framing: Ruby-throated Hummingbird is the only eastern US breeder and definitely uses the property (typical arrival mid-Apr in north GA mountains, departure early Oct).

entries.title: Rabbit Hunting 101 (Georgia DNR Wildlife Resources Division)
entries.framing: State-agency primary source for a species the property plausibly holds. DNR is already the authority this library leans on for wildlife.

entries.title: Gray Squirrel fact sheet (Georgia DNR)
entries.framing: The squirrel is already a tracked mammal on the property. This is the state agency's own account of it, which outranks any general-interest write-up.

entries.title: Georgia squirrel hunting season opens August 15 (Georgia DNR Law Enforcement)
entries.framing: A **dated, seasonal** fact about the property's own calendar — mid-August is inside the window the field journal already narrates.

entries.title: Five squirrel recipes (Georgia Wildlife Blog)
entries.framing: The other half of small game — DNR treats harvest and table as one subject, and so does the property's own use of it.

entries.title: How to Field Dress a Rabbit (wikiHow)
entries.framing: Practical technique reference. ⚠️ **Not an authority** — general-interest, no agency behind it. Fine for method, never for a fact about Georgia.

entries.title: Skinning a rabbit by hand in under a minute (video)
entries.framing: Same class as the wikiHow entry — technique, not authority.

entries.title: Curing small-animal pelts (Instructables)
entries.framing: Extends small game past the table into use of the whole animal. Community-authored — a seed, not an authority.

entries.title: Wild Harvest Initiative — Quarterly Report (March 2020)
entries.framing: The only source in this group that is *about* wild harvest rather than *how to* — it supplies the framing that connects small game to the property's conservation posture, which the rest of this library already leans toward.

entries.title: USDA NRCS Web Soil Survey
entries.framing: The Fernwood property sits on Blue Ridge mountain soils — likely Edneyville, Ashe, Chestnut, or Junaluska series typical of Pickens County's steep forested slopes.

entries.title: USDA NRCS Soil Data Access (SDA) Web Services
entries.framing: Programmatic alternative to WSS — pulls the soil component for the exact property coordinates instead of manually exporting a report.

entries.title: USGS NWIS Water Services API (Instantaneous Values)
entries.framing: Live stream-gauge data from USGS. The Etowah gauges upstream and downstream of the property carry the watershed-health story.

entries.title: USGS Monitoring Locations — Etowah River near Dawsonville (02389150) & Canton (02392000)
entries.framing: 02389150 is the most representative for "headwaters near my property." 02392000 gives long-term flow context downstream.

entries.title: USGS StreamStats — Georgia
entries.framing: The unnamed creek behind Fernwood is almost certainly ungauged. StreamStats can produce a property-specific watershed area, mean annual flow estimate, and flood frequency.

entries.title: USGS Earthquake Hazards — GeoJSON Feeds & FDSN Event API
entries.framing: Southern Appalachians are seismically quiet but not silent — the 2018 Decatur, TN M4.4 was felt across north Georgia. A field-journal cue noting recent regional quakes adds character without being alarmist.

entries.title: Georgia EPD Watershed Protection Branch — TMDLs and 303(d) Listings
entries.framing: Tells you whether your specific Etowah headwater tributary or downstream Lake Sequoyah is listed as impaired (sediment, fecal coliform, biota), directly informing the "support local wildlife and plants" goal.

entries.title: USDA NRCS EQIP — Georgia
entries.framing: "Support local wildlife and plants, especially indigenous" maps directly to EQIP forestry practices. Pickens County is fully eligible; sign-ups continuous, with annual ranking cutoffs.

entries.title: USDA NRCS Conservation Stewardship Program (CSP) — Georgia
entries.framing: Complements EQIP — pays for ongoing stewardship rather than one-time installation, fitting an owner managing the property long-term for wildlife.

entries.title: USDA NRCS Plants Database
entries.framing: Direct way to confirm which species are documented as native to Pickens County — exactly what "indigenous" needs.

entries.title: Coosa River Basin Initiative (CRBI)
entries.framing: The property drains directly into Etowah headwaters → Coosa basin. CRBI publishes the Etowah River User's Guide and runs Adopt-A-Stream and pollution litigation work locally.

entries.title: Upper Etowah River Alliance (UERA)
entries.framing: Most geographically specific watershed group for the property. Pickens County is one of UERA's five core counties; the upper Etowah's 92 native fish species and 5 endemics are core to the conservation story.

entries.title: Mountain Conservation Trust of Georgia (MCT)
entries.framing: MCT's geographic mandate covers this region exactly. The closest-aligned land trust if a conservation easement on Church Mountain Road ever makes sense.

entries.title: Georgia Forestry Commission — Forest Stewardship Program
entries.framing: The free management plan is the practical entry point to most other programs (EQIP cost-share, Tree Farm certification, property tax conservation use). Pickens County is served.

entries.title: USDA Climate Hubs — Southeast Region
entries.framing: The Southern Appalachian forest section of the SE Hub's Vulnerability Assessment is directly applicable to a 2,873 ft Blue Ridge property thinking about long-term species shifts.

entries.title: Georgia-Alabama Land Trust (GALT)
entries.framing: Alternative or complement to MCT for conservation easements. Larger geographic reach but less North-Georgia-specific than MCT.

entries.title: MountainTrue
entries.framing: Pickens isn't yet in MountainTrue's GA service area, but their Southern Blue Ridge work on Nantahala-Pisgah and forest policy affects upstream conditions here.

entries.title: The Nature Conservancy — Upper Coosa River Basin (Georgia)
entries.framing: Frames the property within the Upper Coosa biodiversity story; the Etowah and Conasauga are sister sub-basins of the same system.

entries.title: Cement Pond Tips (Van Ness Water Gardens)
entries.framing: Fernwood's `pond-area` is a real zone with plants and fish downstream of it. The free-lime caution is the load-bearing item here: a newly worked concrete pond can be lethal until it is cured and neutralised.

entries.title: Building a concrete pond (The Concrete Society, UK)
entries.framing: The engineering counterpart to the nursery guidance above: same subject, materially higher authority. ⚠️ UK standards — mixes and terminology differ from US practice; use it for principle, not for a spec.

entries.title: Admixtures as Waterproofing (WATERPROOF! Magazine)
entries.framing: The third approach to the same problem, and the one with the fewest failure modes over time because there is no coating to fail. Trade press, so: informed, but commercially adjacent.

entries.title: Georgia DNR WRD — Trout Fishing & Stocking
entries.framing: Pickens County borders the seasonal trout zone, and Chattahoochee NF streams within ~30 minutes of the property (Amicalola, Cartecay, Mountaintown Creek, Rock Creek) are stocked. Drives "best months" timing for trout.

entries.title: Georgia DNR WRD — Fisheries Management
entries.framing: Source of truth for bass/crappie/bluegill/catfish regulations. Lake Sequoyah is small and likely private — verify whether GA fishing license rules apply or whether HOA-regulated.

entries.title: Georgia Fishing Regulations (eRegulations)
entries.framing: Lake Sequoyah's species list maps directly to specific GA creel/length rules.

entries.title: USFWS Chattahoochee Forest National Fish Hatchery
entries.framing: Closest-fact "where do the trout come from" anchor for the field-journal voice.

entries.title: Blue Ridge Mountain Trout Unlimited (Chapter 696)
entries.framing: Closest TU chapter to Pickens County / Jasper. The Georgia Foothills chapter is further east despite its name.

entries.title: USGS NWIS Water Services API — Stream Temperature & Flow for Trout Habitat
entries.framing: The Fishing tab can pull live water temp from the nearest gauge with that parameter. Water-temp percentile rounds out the field-journal feel.

entries.title: Tennessee Aquarium Conservation Institute (TNACI) — Freshwater Information Network
entries.framing: **The Etowah and Cherokee Darters are *only* found in the Etowah system that drains the property — federally listed and a marquee biodiversity story** for the Wildlife card. TNACI does the propagation work.

entries.title: Conasauga River Alliance
entries.framing: Sister Coosa-basin watershed one ridge west; useful regional context, not the property's direct watershed.

entries.title: Southeastern Fishes Council (SFC)
entries.framing: Primary scholarly venue for Etowah/Coosa endemic-fish research.

entries.title: North American Native Fishes Association (NANFA)
entries.framing: Hobbyist-friendly entry point to the same darter/minnow biodiversity story TNACI works on professionally; good for the field-journal personal-naturalist tone.

entries.title: USGS BioData — Aquatic Bioassessment
entries.framing: Source for actual fish-community survey data in the Etowah basin — "what species have actually been caught here" beyond stocking lists. **Caveat:** retrieval site has had recurring availability issues — verify before depending on it.

entries.title: USFWS Partnership for the Upper Coosa
entries.framing: Federal-side counterpart to state and nonprofit Coosa-basin work; useful for ESA-listed species framing.

entries.title: Georgia Rivers (formerly Georgia River Network)
entries.framing: Single jumping-off point for Georgia watershed groups; their Coosa River page is a clean basin summary.

entries.title: Old-School Tips for Catching Giant Bass in Small Ponds (Outdoor Life)
entries.framing: ⚠️ **Scope note worth keeping straight:** `fishing.json` is built around **Lake Sequoyah**, not the property pond. This is the only source in the library aimed at the *pond*, and it is only useful if the pond is actually fished — which the record does not currently say either way.

entries.title: Boating Knots (Animated Knots by Grog)
entries.framing: General utility around water and equipment rather than fishing specifically. Included because it is genuinely useful and permanently free; filed here because water is where it gets used.

entries.title: NOAA NCEI Climate Data Online (CDO)
entries.framing: Long-term context for the Ambient Weather station's live readings. What does a "normal" May look like at this elevation, and how is the current month tracking?

entries.title: NOAA NWS API (api.weather.gov)
entries.framing: Bortle 3 here — sky-cover forecast is the astronomy variable that matters most. Open-Meteo gives a model blend; NWS gives the official forecaster's grid.

entries.title: PRISM Climate Group (Oregon State)
entries.framing: At 2,873 ft on a Blue Ridge ridge, the closest NWS station (likely valley-floor Jasper or Blairsville) doesn't represent your microclimate. PRISM's 800m grid actually captures the elevation gradient.

entries.title: Southeast Regional Climate Center (SERCC)
entries.framing: Answers "is this May unusually wet/dry/cool for north Georgia?" against the historical record. The SERCC Climate Perspectives tool (https://sercc.oasis.unc.edu/) compares the current period to climatology.

entries.title: Southeast Climate Adaptation Science Center (USGS)
entries.framing: Goes beyond historical normals into "what's coming" — projections for Southern Appalachian temperature, precip regime shifts, forest-ecosystem response. Directly relevant to the "support local wildlife and plants" goal under shifting conditions.

entries.title: NOAA Climate Resilience Toolkit Climate Explorer
entries.framing: Pickens County has its own page — temperature/precipitation projections through end of century are pre-rendered. Most accessible "what does Pickens County look like in 2050?" view.

entries.title: US Drought Monitor / Drought.gov
entries.framing: Pickens County drought status directly affects watering decisions, fire risk, and what wildlife is pressuring water sources on the property.

entries.title: DarkSky International
entries.framing: Property at Bortle 3 — a top tier this far east. Establishes vocabulary, certification context, lighting principles a homesteader could voluntarily adopt to preserve the asset.

entries.title: Stephen C. Foster State Park (Georgia's only IDA Dark Sky Park)
entries.framing: Useful Bortle reference point ("Stephen C. Foster is Bortle 2; here at Church Mountain Road we're Bortle 3"). A calibrated "darker than here" destination.

entries.title: Atlanta Astronomy Club (and Deerlick Astronomy Village)
entries.framing: Nearest organized astronomy community for a Pickens County stargazer.

entries.title: NASA Scientific Visualization Studio — Moon Phase & Eclipse Pages
entries.framing: Public-domain Moon imagery, refreshed hourly. **The March 3, 2026 total lunar eclipse is visible from Georgia** — featured-event candidate.

entries.title: International Meteor Organization (IMO) Meteor Shower Calendar
entries.framing: Bortle 3 is genuinely good meteor-watching territory — you can actually see the showers. The 2026 calendar with Moon phase correlation is exactly what the celestial card should highlight.

entries.title: American Meteor Society
entries.framing: Cross-reference for IMO data; sometimes phrased better for journal-tone copy.

entries.title: Stellarium Web
entries.framing: When a meteor shower or planetary conjunction shows up on the dashboard, the user wants to know "where do I look?" Stellarium answers for any lat/lon and time.

entries.title: Open-Meteo cloud cover (already integrated)
entries.framing: No key, free, CORS-enabled. Pair with NWS skyCover for redundancy/cross-check.

entries.title: Time and Date AS — sun/moon reference
entries.framing: Free, human-readable cross-check. Skip the API; reference link only.

entries.title: AirNow API
entries.framing: Southern Appalachians get smoke from prescribed burns and from western US wildfires that drift east. AirNow tells you when it's a "stay inside" day vs. fine.

entries.title: Georgia Forestry Commission — Burn Permits & Interactive Map
entries.framing: **Pickens County has a state summer open burning ban May 1 – Sep 30** (Georgia EPD rule). Outside that window, permit required for most burns.

entries.title: Southern Fire Exchange
entries.framing: If the owner ever considers prescribed fire (a real management option in Southern Appalachian forests for wildlife and oak regeneration), SFE is the science source.

entries.title: ATTRA Sustainable Agriculture (NCAT) — Appalachian publications
entries.framing: Written for working ground at this elevation and ecosystem — practical Southern Appalachian land management. Free PDFs.

entries.title: Southern SARE
entries.framing: Funding pathway if the property's wildlife/native-plant goals scale to a research-worthy project. Free online learning library (cover crops, agroforestry, pollinators).

entries.title: Appalachian Sustainable Development (ASD)
entries.framing: Shade-grown, native-forest agroforestry is exactly the model for a wooded mountain property aiming to "support local wildlife and plants, especially indigenous." Pawpaw, elderberry, ramps, ginseng all native to your forest type.

entries.title: Appalachian Beginning Forest Farmer Coalition
entries.framing: Bortle 3, 2,873 ft, Blue Ridge mature forest — textbook habitat for shade-grown native NTFPs. They run trainings and a mentorship network.

entries.title: Carolina Farm Stewardship Association
entries.framing: Closest regional analog organization to GA. North Georgia mountains share more growing-condition DNA with western NC than south Georgia.

entries.title: Appalachian Beekeepers Association of Georgia (Pickens-area chapter)
entries.framing: A Pickens County beekeepers' chapter — closer to the property than anything else on this shelf. Bees do the work of pollinating the natives we tend.

entries.title: UGA Bee Program
entries.framing: State-level technical backstop. Useful for variety selection (Italian vs. Russian for north GA winters), Varroa management timing tied to local nectar flows.

entries.title: Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians — Natural Resources & Center for Cherokee Plants
entries.framing: **Pickens County was Cherokee Nation territory from 1793–1838 (Trail of Tears removal).** The plants the Cherokee cultivated and tended for 6,000+ years — white oak, ramps (wasdi), sochan, ginseng, river cane — are still the native plants of this property. The single most authentic frame for "indigenous plants" on this land.

entries.title: USDA Forest Service × EBCI — Culturally Significant Plants Research
entries.framing: Pickens County sits at the southern end of this same forest ecosystem. The same plant-management principles apply on Church Mountain Road. A real-world model of indigenous-led land stewardship.

entries.title: Family email archive — Tate Mountain community record (2010–2026) 🏠 primary source
entries.framing: Every other source in this category is *about* Tate; this one is the family *in* Tate — the lived-membership layer that connects the Sam Tate history to the Property card's present. TMC minutes are also the community's own governance record (roads, dam, pond, boundaries) — the authoritative source for community-infrastructure facts near the property.

entries.title: Pickens County, Georgia (New Georgia Encyclopedia)
entries.framing: The single most reliable secondary source for the property's county-level historical context. Use as the anchor citation when sourcing any Pickens history claim on the Property card.

entries.title: Marble (New Georgia Encyclopedia)
entries.framing: Frames why the property's host town exists. "Tate" is literally a marble-industry company town.

entries.title: Georgia Marble Company (New Georgia Encyclopedia)
entries.framing: Col. Sam Tate is the same person who built Tate Mountain Estates — the development the property sits within. Reading this article makes the property feel intentional, not incidental.

entries.title: "Tate and Foremen" — Marble Varieties (New Georgia Encyclopedia)
entries.framing: When pointing out the marble in the Tate House (now a wedding venue), the Connahaynee Lodge's baths, the Tate Cemetery monuments, or the Pickens County Courthouse — you can name the variety.

entries.title: Georgia Historical Society Marker — "Georgia Marble Company and the Village of Tate"
entries.framing: A physical, visit-able primary source ~5 minutes from the property. Photograph and link from Property card.

entries.title: Talking Rock (New Georgia Encyclopedia)
entries.framing: This is the most specific, named Cherokee place adjacent to the property. The "indigenous land" framing in the dashboard rests on the Sanderstown / Carmel Mission / Fort Newman triad, not abstract "Cherokee Nation" territory. Cherokee settlements clustered along Talking Rock Creek, Talona Creek, and Long Swamp Creek — all within ~10 mi of the property.

entries.title: Civil War Dissent (New Georgia Encyclopedia)
entries.framing: The "Union flag at the courthouse for a month after secession" story is one of the property's most distinctive regional facts.

entries.title: Sequoyah (New Georgia Encyclopedia)
entries.framing: The lake adjacent to the property bears his name. Knowing what he actually did — and that he never lived here — sharpens both the Property card naming story and the cultural-context disclaimer.

entries.title: Pickens Historical Society (formerly Marble Valley Historical Society)
entries.framing: Three visit-able historical sites within ~20 min of the property; primary archive for Pickens County materials.

entries.title: Mount Oglethorpe Foundation / Eagles Rest Park
entries.framing: The property sits on the same range. This is one of the most striking layered-history moments in the area: a 21-year period when through-hikers ended (or began) their 2,200-mile journey on a mountain the Cherokee had settled since the 1700s, on land bought by the marble baron who also developed Tate Mountain Estates. The terminus moved 13 mi NE to Springer Mountain in 1958 after logging operations, chicken ranches, and a gravel road brought vandalism.

entries.title: "The Connahaynee Lodge (1930-1946)" — North Georgia History
entries.framing: The most specific, vivid period-detail source on what Tate Mountain Estates actually was when it was new. Multiple Property-card anecdotes come from here.

entries.title: Tate Mountain Estates — Pickens Past
entries.framing: The longest-running local-history blog focused specifically on this development.

entries.title: "Placenames, Gone but not Forgotten" — Don & Diane Wells, Mountain Stewards
entries.framing: Primary place-name reference for the small geography immediately around the property.

entries.title: Old Federal Road — Phase I Historical Context Study (GDOT)
entries.framing: Authoritative academic source for the Federal Road's specific Pickens routing. Andrew Jackson and James Monroe both traveled this road through what is now the property's county.

entries.title: Native American History of Pickens County (Access Genealogy)
entries.framing: Compiled genealogy/history article covering Cherokee presence in Pickens County. Useful complement to the New Georgia Encyclopedia for primary-source Cherokee references and family lines.

entries.title: "Black History in Pickens" — Pickens Progress
entries.framing: Counters a Sam-Tate-centric reading of the marble story with the laborers' perspective. The "first electrified town" was electrified for and by them too.

entries.title: USGS Indigenous Knowledge / Tribal Climate Resources
entries.framing: Honest framing for a non-Cherokee owner: how to learn from and credit Indigenous Knowledges respectfully rather than appropriating. Case-study library includes Southern Appalachian examples.

entries.title: Visit Pickens GA — Community Calendar
entries.framing: Pickens County's events aggregator. First stop when refreshing `events.json` or spot-checking a date.

entries.title: Know Pickens — Events Calendar
entries.framing: Backup verification source for Pickens County dates.

entries.title: Explore Georgia — State Calendar of Events
entries.framing: State-level cross-check for any event that draws regional attention; useful for picking up events outside Pickens (Ellijay, Blue Ridge, Dahlonega).

entries.title: Pickens County Chamber of Commerce — Events & Marble Festival
entries.framing: Official site for the marquee annual Pickens event. Anchored in the property's local-history thread.

entries.title: Sheriff's JeepFest
entries.framing: Largest Pickens summer event aside from JeepFest's flagship sub-events. Has its own community draw.

entries.title: Talking Rock Heritage Days
entries.framing: Walk-distance scale from the Talking Rock Cherokee history (Cat 7's Sanderstown / Carmel Mission / Fort Newman triad). Combine with a Federal Road / Hwy 136 bridge visit.

entries.title: Jasper Pro Rodeo — Pickens County Stampede
entries.framing: Brief, single-evening attendance option in May.

entries.title: Georgia Apple Festival (Ellijay)
entries.framing: Ellijay is ~30 min from the property; the Apple Festival overlaps with peak fall color and Marble Festival/Heritage Days.

entries.title: Downtown Ellijay & Gilmer Chamber — Events
entries.framing: Adds recurring weekly market data and winter holiday events to the calendar.

entries.title: Blue Ridge Mountains EDA — Events Calendar
entries.framing: Strongest single-county events list for Fannin. Blue Ridge edges the day-trip radius but the Blue Ridge Scenic Railway anchor + festival density make it worth the drive.

entries.title: Discover Dahlonega — Festivals
entries.framing: Dahlonega is GA wine country; Bear on the Square is a marquee Appalachian-tradition festival.

entries.title: Pickens Past — Tate Day & Local History Events
entries.framing: Source for "Tate Day" and other history-society-driven events that the chamber calendar may not pick up.
